claim: When a jailbreak attack succeeds against a safety-aligned LLM, the model's safety-relevant internal representations are not eliminated — they are bypassed. The attack selectively suppresses a small subset of attention heads, and suppressing that subset is by itself enough to turn a refusal into a compliance, while other heads go on representing the harmful content even as the attack succeeds. Because those representations persist, they can be read out directly as a harmful-input detector, with no additional training, at a quality competitive with dedicated safety models.
experiments_evaluated: To address subclaim "What happens to a safety-aligned LLM’s safety-relevant internal representations when a jailbreak attack succeeds?" and the paired subclaims "Are the model’s safety-relevant internal representations eliminated during a successful jailbreak attack?" and "Are the model’s safety-relevant internal representations bypassed during a successful jailbreak attack?", run a representational comparison study on a publicly available safety-aligned model and jailbreak benchmark. Use a model such as Llama-2-7b-chat or Mistral-7B-Instruct, and prompts from HarmBench, AdvBench, and JailbreakBench (all public). Construct matched prompt sets: benign, plainly harmful, and harmful-with-jailbreak-suffix/prefix that empirically convert refusals into compliant answers. For each prompt, record hidden states and attention-head outputs across layers while generating the first refusal/compliance tokens. First identify candidate safety-relevant directions by contrasting activations for benign vs harmful non-jailbroken prompts that the model refuses; this can be done with simple unsupervised or linear-probe-free diagnostics such as mean-difference directions, CKA similarity to harmful/non-harmful centroids, or activation steering directions derived only from class means. Then test whether those directions disappear under successful jailbreaks or remain present. Also quantify whether the final behavior shifts despite persistence of those directions. A key control is to compare successful jailbreaks against unsuccessful jailbreak attempts and against direct harmful prompts answered with refusal. If the harmful-associated directions remain strong under successful jailbreaks, while output behavior changes from refusal to compliance, that supports the "bypass" view rather than elimination. If those directions collapse to benign-like values during successful jailbreaks, that supports elimination. Intermediate results, such as persistence in mid-layers but disappearance near the output, would suggest partial bypass localized late in computation rather than global preservation. This experiment is highest priority because it establishes whether there is anything persistent to read out or causally intervene on. It could be made partly unnecessary if strong prior evidence already included layerwise activation traces on matched harmful, jailbroken, and benign prompts showing persistence or disappearance of safety-relevant directions across the network.

To address subclaim "Does the jailbreak attack selectively suppress a small subset of attention heads?" and "Is suppressing that subset of attention heads enough to turn a refusal into compliance?", perform a causal head-ablation and rescue experiment. Using the same public model and jailbreak datasets, first identify attention heads whose outputs change most between harmful-refusal prompts and their successfully jailbroken counterparts; prioritize heads showing large, consistent reduction under jailbreak specifically on harmful inputs. Rank heads by effect size, then intervene at inference time: (1) suppress only the top-k candidate heads during normal harmful prompts that would otherwise be refused, by zeroing or mean-patching their output vectors; (2) restore those same heads during successful jailbreak prompts by activation patching from the matched non-jailbroken harmful-refusal run; and (3) include controls that suppress random head sets of the same size, suppress MLP channels instead, or suppress candidate heads on benign tasks to test specificity. Measure refusal/compliance rate, harmfulness score of completions using a public evaluator or rubric, and perplexity impact on benign tasks from a public corpus such as WikiText or AlpacaEval-style harmless prompts. If suppressing a very small head subset reliably flips refusal to compliance, while random subsets do not, that supports selective suppression being sufficient. If restoring those heads during jailbroken runs reinstates refusal, that strengthens a causal interpretation. If many heads must be suppressed, or random subsets work similarly, the "small selective subset" claim weakens. If suppressing candidate heads broadly degrades model quality, the effect may reflect generic damage rather than safety-specific gating. This experiment could be made less necessary if existing evidence already provided causal activation-patching or ablation results demonstrating both sufficiency and rescue for a compact head set across multiple jailbreak families.

To address subclaim "Do other attention heads continue representing harmful content even when the jailbreak attack succeeds?", "Can the persistent internal representations be read out directly as a harmful-input detector?", "Is additional training required to read out those representations as a harmful-input detector?", and "How does the quality of this harmful-input detector compare with dedicated safety models?", build a zero-additional-training detection benchmark from internal activations. Use public harmfulness datasets such as HarmBench, BeaverTails, ToxicChat, and WildJailbreak/JailbreakBench to create a held-out mixture of benign prompts, harmful prompts, and successfully jailbroken harmful prompts. From the model under test, extract activations from non-suppressed heads and/or layers identified in Experiment 1 as still encoding harmfulness during jailbreak. Define a detector without fitting new parameters on labeled data: for example, score each input by cosine similarity to a harmful centroid computed from a small reference set, by projection onto a precomputed harmful-minus-benign mean direction from the model’s own refusal regime, or by aggregation of head-level harmfulness scores discovered in Experiment 1. Compare this zero-training detector against dedicated public safety classifiers such as Llama Guard, OpenAI moderation analogs where open equivalents exist, Detoxify, or other HuggingFace safety models, using AUROC, AUPRC, F1 at fixed false-positive rate, and robustness specifically on jailbroken prompts. Include a stricter no-training variant where the harmful direction is inferred only from paired harmful/benign prompt templates rather than any supervised fitting, plus a light-training baseline (e.g., logistic regression on frozen activations) to show the gap if any. If the zero-training internal detector performs competitively with dedicated safety models, especially on successfully jailbroken inputs, that supports the claim strongly. If it only works after fitting a classifier, the "no additional training" claim fails but persistence may still hold. If dedicated safety models far outperform it, the competitiveness claim weakens. This experiment becomes less necessary if prior evidence already reports strong held-out benchmarking of a training-free activation-based detector against public safety baselines on standard jailbreak and harmfulness datasets.
reference_experiments: Before identifying any component, test the premise that attacks bypass rather than erase safety representations. On inputs where a jailbreak succeeded, measure activation of the refusal direction across all layers and components (attention heads and MLPs) and compare against the same requests unattacked. If a successful attack flattens refusal activation everywhere, attacks do break safety representations and everything downstream is dead. The authors find mid layers still maintain substantial refusal activation under successful attack, particularly in the layers previously identified as most safety-relevant.

Construct the paired evaluation set the whole analysis depends on. Sample benign prompts from Alpaca, collect harmful behaviours from published harmful-behaviour datasets, generate attack variants with GCG, AutoDAN, many-shot jailbreaking and PAIR, and retain only pairs where the unattacked request is refused and the attacked version succeeds. Within-pair comparison is what separates the attack's effect from differences between requests. The authors obtain 378 (Llama-2-7B-Chat) and 176 (Llama-3-8B-Instruct) usable pairs from roughly 10,000 attack samples, a 2-3% yield that caps the study's statistical power.

Build and calibrate the component-scoring instrument. Extract the refusal direction by difference-in-means and select the optimal layer, project it into each attention head's output space to score that head's contribution to the refusal signal, and classify heads by distribution overlap between conditions using two-stage filtering. Then verify the classification is not an artifact of the cut point by sweeping the threshold and the KDE bandwidth. The authors use thresholds of 0.5, find stability across 0.4-0.6, and obtain 21 ACHs and 17 SAHs for Llama-3 (416 heads analysed) and 20 ACHs and 19 SAHs for Llama-2 (480 analysed), with ACHs concentrated in layers 0-3 and SAHs in layers 5-12.

Test causally whether suppressing the identified heads is sufficient to cause attack success. On harmful inputs the model normally refuses (baseline ASR about 0%), inject a negative refusal-direction feature into ACH outputs, progressively increase the number of intervened heads, and measure attack success rate — with a matched random-head intervention as control, 10 seeds and 95% confidence intervals. Without the random-head arm the effect cannot be attributed to those heads rather than to perturbing that many heads at all. The authors report ACH intervention driving ASR to 99.5% (Llama-3) and 83.7% (Llama-2), reaching 95.0% and 81.6% at just 8 heads, against 4.0% +/- 3.7 and 10.2% +/- 11.6 for random heads.

Test whether the other head type is a real source of the persistent signal. Apply the same suppression to SAHs, this time on attack inputs, and measure the change in mid-layer activation strength using mean absolute activation across mid-layer heads. The authors report Llama-2 falling from 0.222 to 0.181 (18%) and Llama-3 from 0.0062 to 0.0053 (14%), against a reference of 0.397 and 0.0086 under unattacked harmful inputs.

Discriminate the mechanistic account from the rival explanation that the two head types simply differ in sensitivity to harmful content. Using the linearity of attention, attribute each head's activation to individual input tokens, separate the contribution of the original harmful-request tokens from that of the attack-template tokens, and compare the two head types on each. The account holds only if the types are indistinguishable on the harmful request itself and separate sharply on the attack template. The authors report medians within +/-0.15 on harmful tokens, against roughly -1.5 for ACHs and +1.5 for SAHs on attack-template tokens.

Validate externally that the persistent signal generalises and is useful. Build a training-free detector that reads standardised activations at discriminative positions via top-m aggregation and thresholds the score, then evaluate Macro-F1 on ten safety-eval benchmarks across six models from three architecture families, against both the model's own refusal behaviour and trained guard models. If the readout does not transfer, the phenomenon is a property of the two models analysed. The authors report Gemma-2B improving from 0.470 to 0.853 and Qwen-7B from 0.506 to 0.860 overall, SALAD-Bench from 0.270 to 0.976, and Llama-3-8B reaching 0.888 weighted average against WildGuard 0.880 and LlamaGuard3/4 at 0.599/0.666.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A matched, layer- and component-resolved measure of safety-related activation under successful jailbreaks versus the same requests without the jailbreak, capable of distinguishing persistence from global erasure.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 explicitly records hidden states and attention-head outputs across layers on matched refused and successfully jailbroken harmful prompts, identifies harmful/safety-associated directions, and tests whether they persist or collapse. It also measures the behavioral shift, so the team could decide bypass versus elimination.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A paired evaluation population containing harmful requests that are refused normally and matched attack versions that succeed, so attack effects can be separated from differences in the underlying requests.
reference_coverage.rationale: Experiment 0 specifies matched plainly harmful and successfully jailbroken prompts, with unsuccessful attempts and refusal controls; experiment 1 and experiment 2 reuse the same matched public prompt/attack resources. The proposed set therefore supplies the within-request refused-versus-successful comparisons needed for the analysis, without needing the reference paper's exact datasets or attack counts.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A reproducible component-level criterion for identifying attack-suppressed safety heads and unaffected heads, with selection robust enough that the result is not just an arbitrary cutoff or perturbation choice.
reference_coverage.rationale: Experiment 1 ranks heads by consistent jailbreak-specific output changes and tests compact top-k sets with random-head, MLP, and benign-task controls; experiment 2 separately uses the non-suppressed heads. This provides an alternative operational way to identify and distinguish the relevant head subsets and test whether the distinction is meaningful.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A causal intervention on a compact candidate head set during normally refused harmful inputs, with same-size perturbation controls, that can establish whether those heads alone are sufficient to flip refusal into compliance.
reference_coverage.rationale: Experiment 1 directly suppresses the top-k candidate heads on harmful prompts that otherwise elicit refusals, varies the compact set size, measures compliance and harmfulness, and includes matched random-head and MLP controls. Its planned rescue intervention is an additional causal check rather than a requirement for sufficiency.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Causal evidence that heads outside the selectively suppressed group remain a source of the safety-relevant signal under successful attack, rather than the residual signal being only an artifact of the targeted heads.
reference_coverage.rationale: Experiment 0 directly measures whether safety-associated activations persist in the non-targeted components during successful jailbreaks, and Experiment 2 tests whether activations from those components carry harmful-input information. However, the proposed set does not explicitly suppress that remaining group and measure the resulting loss of the persistent signal, so it cannot cleanly establish the causal source contribution tested by the reference.
reasoning_chain: [1] The reference experiment establishes the contribution of the non-targeted head group by suppressing that group and measuring a corresponding reduction in the mid-layer safety signal.
[2] Proposed experiment 0 can show that non-targeted activations remain present, and proposed experiment 2 can show that they are decodable during jailbreaks.
[3] Persistence and decodability establish retained information but do not distinguish causal contribution from correlation or information inherited from other components.
[4] A team running the proposed set would therefore remain uncertain whether the other heads are the causal source of the persistent signal: partial.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A token-resolved discrimination showing that the two head types are similarly responsive to the original harmful request but differ specifically in their handling of jailbreak-template tokens, ruling out simple baseline sensitivity to harmful content as the explanation.
reference_coverage.rationale: The matched-prompt comparisons and harmful/benign specificity controls bear on whether head changes are jailbreak-specific, but the proposed set does not attribute activations to original harmful-request tokens versus attack-template tokens. reference_coverage.rationale: Experiment 2 constructs a held-out mixture spanning multiple public harmfulness and jailbreak resources, includes an explicitly no-fitting detector variant, evaluates jailbroken robustness with AUROC/AUPRC/F1 and fixed-false-positive-rate metrics, and compares against public dedicated safety classifiers. sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set would directly test persistence versus elimination, identify and causally suppress a compact head subset with controls, test whether other heads retain readable harmfulness information, and benchmark a no-additional-training detector against dedicated safety models.
